prompt: In its default way of paying, what is an Athena query billed by?
hint: There is no cluster to leave running.

choices.text: The seconds the query took to run
choices.why: Time is how a warehouse cluster is paid for; Athena's per-query price does not look at the clock.

choices.text: The bytes it read from S3
choices.why: Right: 9 dollars a terabyte in São Paulo, rounded up to whole megabytes.

choices.text: The number of rows in its answer
choices.why: A query that reads a whole bucket to return four rows pays for the bucket.

choices.text: The hours its workgroup was enabled
choices.why: A workgroup is a set of settings and costs nothing while it waits.

prompt: Athena rounds the bytes a query read up to a whole megabyte, and charges at least ___ MB for any query.
hint: It is the number three of the four bills in this lesson met.

prompt: Tonight a file for 2026-10-16 lands under the table's `LOCATION`, in `dt=2026-10-16/`. Tomorrow a query with `WHERE dt = '2026-10-16'` returns no rows. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Where does Athena find the list of partitions?

choices.text: A new object in S3 takes a day to become readable
choices.why: S3 reads back a new object at once; the delay is not in S3.

choices.text: The file has to be loaded into Athena with a `COPY` first
choices.why: That is a warehouse's way. Athena reads the files where they are.

choices.text: Nobody added the partition to the catalog
choices.why: Right. Until `MSCK REPAIR TABLE`, `ADD PARTITION`, a crawler or a projection names it, Athena does not read that prefix.

choices.text: Athena answered from a cached result of yesterday's query
choices.why: Reusing results is a setting that is off unless turned on, and the query had a different filter.

prompt: You run `DROP TABLE quitanda.orders` on the external table of `orders.sql`. What happens to the objects under `s3://quitanda-curated-prod/orders/`?
hint: Whose data is it, according to `EXTERNAL`?

choices.text: They are deleted with the table
choices.why: That is what dropping a managed table does; an external one owns only its description.

choices.text: They stay where they are
choices.why: Right. Only the description in the catalog goes, and a new `CREATE` reads the same files again.

choices.text: They move to the workgroup's results prefix
choices.why: Athena writes answers there; it moves nothing of yours.

choices.text: They are kept for 30 days and then expire
choices.why: Expiry is a life-cycle rule on the bucket, lesson 3, and a table cannot set one.

prompt: Which of these cost nothing on Athena's per-terabyte price? Choose all that apply.
hint: What does a statement read from S3?

choices.text: A `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE` statement
choices.why: Yes: a statement that only changes the catalog is free.

choices.text: An `ALTER TABLE … ADD PARTITION`
choices.why: Yes, for the same reason.

choices.text: A query that fails on a column that does not exist
choices.why: Yes: failed queries are not charged.

choices.text: A query you cancel after it has read 2 GB
choices.why: A cancelled query costs what it had read when it stopped.

choices.text: A query that reads 50 MB and returns no rows
choices.why: The read is the bill, whatever came out of it.

prompt: moto answers `DDL` and `SUCCEEDED` for `orders.sql`, and `aws glue get-databases` comes back empty. What does that prove about `orders.sql`?
hint: What did moto keep?

choices.text: That it is valid Athena DDL and would create the table
choices.why: Athena would have refused it, since the database `quitanda` does not exist.

choices.text: That moto created the table in another region
choices.why: moto created nothing anywhere; it marked the request done.

choices.text: Only that the request was well formed
choices.why: Right. moto ran no DDL, and a success from it is a statement about the request.

choices.text: That Athena keeps its tables outside the Glue Data Catalog
choices.why: Athena's tables live in the Glue Data Catalog; it is moto that kept no table.

prompt: Why does `lake.py` read `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` itself and hand the address to PyArrow?
hint: Which programs read that variable on their own?

choices.text: PyArrow does not read it, and without it would go to the real S3
choices.why: Right. The variable is read by the AWS command line and boto3, and PyArrow needs `endpoint_override`.

choices.text: moto refuses a request whose address does not carry the port number
choices.why: The port is part of the address the variable holds; the issue is who reads the variable.

choices.text: To keep the two keys `test` out of the source code of the program itself
choices.why: The keys are other variables, which PyArrow does read.

choices.text: So that the region becomes `sa-east-1`
choices.why: The region comes from `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`, another line of the program.

prompt: The same 755,511 orders take 40,641,097 bytes as CSV and 12,703,975 as Parquet. Where does the saving come from?
hint: Nothing was lost on the way.

choices.text: Parquet leaves out the partition column `dt`
choices.why: Neither file holds `dt`: it is in the key for both layers.

choices.text: Parquet rounds `total_cents` to whole reais
choices.why: Every value survives; both layers give the same sums to the cent.

choices.text: Columns stored apart, with their types, and compressed with Snappy
choices.why: Right. A column of small numbers in one place compresses far better than the same numbers spread through lines of text.

choices.text: `lake.py` writes fewer days to the curated layer
choices.why: It printed 31 objects for each layer.

prompt: In this lake, what is the difference between the raw layer and the curated layer?
hint: Same rows, two buckets.

choices.text: Raw is the development copy and curated is the production copy
choices.why: Both are `-prod`; the environment is the last word of the name.

choices.text: Raw keeps a sample of the orders and curated keeps every one of them
choices.why: Both hold all 755,511 orders.

choices.text: Raw is encrypted and curated is not
choices.why: Nothing in this lesson sets encryption on either bucket.

choices.text: Raw is what arrives, as CSV; curated is what is read, as Parquet
choices.why: Right. Lesson 17 is the job that turns one into the other.

prompt: How does `ask.py` know how many bytes a query read?
hint: Look at what `Counted` stands between.

choices.text: It asks moto's Athena for `DataScannedInBytes`
choices.why: moto answers 0 for every query, which is why the program exists.

choices.text: Every read PyArrow makes from S3 passes through it and is added up
choices.why: Right. The count is made where the bytes pass, so a column nobody read adds nothing.

choices.text: It estimates the size from the columns that the SQL names
choices.why: Nothing is estimated; the footer bytes it counted are the proof.

choices.text: It adds up the object sizes that `aws s3 ls` prints for the prefix
choices.why: That would give the whole table every time, and the counts differ per question.

prompt: The question about payments names two of the seven columns, and on the CSV the read was all 40,641,097 bytes. Why?
hint: Where does a column start in a line of text?

choices.text: The `ORDER BY` forced the engine to read everything
choices.why: The sort is over four result rows; the Parquet read with the same `ORDER BY` was eight times smaller.

choices.text: A CSV file gives no way to find a column without reading each line whole
choices.why: Right. Every line was read to pick two values out of it.

choices.text: `ask.py` reads every object whole, whatever its format
choices.why: On Parquet it read 5,102,048 bytes of 12,703,975.

choices.text: The question had no `WHERE`, and a query without one reads every column of a table
choices.why: A filter decides which rows or partitions; which columns are read is the format's business.

prompt: A day written a minute ago shows up in `ask.py`'s answer and not in Athena's, for the same SQL over the same objects. Why?
hint: Each one finds the partitions in a different place.

choices.text: S3 shows a newly written object to some readers a while before it shows it to others
choices.why: S3 reads a new object back at once to everybody.

choices.text: Athena answers from its own copy of the lake, which it refreshes once every night
choices.why: Athena keeps no copy; it reads the objects at query time.

choices.text: `ask.py` lists S3 each run, while the catalog decides which days the other reads
choices.why: Right. The new day is in S3 and not yet in the catalog.

choices.text: DuckDB reads Parquet files that Athena's engine is not able to read
choices.why: Both read the same Parquet; the difference is which files each was told about.

prompt: With `WHERE dt = '2026-10-15'` the engine opened one object of 31. What made skipping the other 30 possible?
hint: Where is `dt` written?

choices.text: `dt` is in the key, so the filter is settled before any read
choices.why: Right, and it works on the CSV too, which also opened one object.

choices.text: The smallest and largest value in each Parquet footer
choices.why: Those let a reader skip blocks inside a file it opened; the CSV, which has no footer, skipped the same 30 days.

choices.text: DuckDB kept the other days from an earlier query
choices.why: Each run of `ask.py` is a new process with nothing kept.

choices.text: The days were sorted by date, so the engine stopped at the 15th
choices.why: An engine that stopped there would still have opened the fourteen days before it.

prompt: The query on `hour` read 2,039,661 bytes from 31 objects, and PyArrow read each footer as 65,536 bytes. How many bytes were the `hour` column itself?
hint: Take 31 footers away.

prompt: Why does the part of a Parquet read spent on footers grow with the number of files rather than with their size?
hint: How many footers does a file have?

choices.text: A footer holds a copy of every value of the file
choices.why: It holds a map of where each column block is: 1,576 bytes for a day of 23,781 rows.

choices.text: PyArrow rereads the footer before each column it reads
choices.why: One footer read per object: the hour query made 62 requests to 31 objects, two each.

choices.text: Each file is read for its own footer once, whatever its size
choices.why: Right: 31 files, 31 footer reads. A hundred small files per day would be a hundred per day.

choices.text: Larger files are compressed better, so their footers become smaller
choices.why: A footer's size follows the number of columns and blocks, not the compression.

prompt: Three of the four questions were billed the same 10 MB although their reads differ by a factor of 31. What is the right reading of that?
hint: Multiply the lake by a thousand.

choices.text: Partitioning saves nothing on Athena, only on DuckDB
choices.why: On a lake a thousand times larger the reads keep their ratios and the bills follow them.

choices.text: The lake is small, so the minimum hides ratios that a larger lake pays in full
choices.why: Right. At a thousand times this lake, the dashboard was 1,485 dollars a month against 186.

choices.text: Parquet costs the same as CSV on Athena once both kinds of file are compressed
choices.why: The CSV month was billed 39 MB against the Parquet's 10, on the same rows.

choices.text: `ask.py` rounds its counts to whole megabytes and so loses the difference
choices.why: It counts every byte; only the bill is rounded, by Athena's own rule.

prompt: On AWS, what happens to a query in the `analysts` workgroup, with its 10 MB cutoff, that would read the 40,641,097 bytes of the CSV month?
hint: moto recorded the setting and did nothing with it.

choices.text: It runs to the end and the bill stops at 10 MB
choices.why: The cutoff ends the query; it does not give away the rest of the read.

choices.text: It is refused before reading, since the table is larger than the cutoff
choices.why: Athena cannot know in advance what a query will read; it counts as it goes.

choices.text: It succeeds, because the cutoff only applies to the console
choices.why: The cutoff belongs to the workgroup and applies to every query run in it.

choices.text: It is cancelled once its scan passes 10 MB
choices.why: Right, and the person who ran it gets an error naming the limit.

prompt: What does partition projection change about how Athena finds a table's partitions?
hint: Look at `storage.location.template`.

choices.text: A crawler runs before each query and registers the days that arrived since the last
choices.why: No crawler is involved: the catalog is left out of the question.

choices.text: It computes the keys from the table's properties instead of looking them up
choices.why: Right. Tonight's day is readable with nothing registered, as long as its key fits the template.

choices.text: Partitions are copied into Athena so that it can skip S3
choices.why: Athena keeps no data; it still reads the objects in S3.

choices.text: It merges the small partitions into larger ones, on a schedule of its own choosing
choices.why: Projection changes how keys are found, not the files under them.

prompt: Quitanda wants three years of daily CSV turned into Parquet partitioned by `dt`, with Athena alone. Why will one CTAS statement not do it?
hint: Count the partitions.

choices.text: CTAS writes CSV only, so a second statement would have to convert it to Parquet
choices.why: CTAS writes the format named in `WITH`, Parquet included.

choices.text: CTAS cannot partition its output
choices.why: `partitioned_by` is one of its properties.

choices.text: A CTAS is capped at 10 MB, which is the minimum a query is billed for on Athena
choices.why: The minimum is the least a query is billed, not the most it reads.

choices.text: It writes at most 100 partitions, and three years is over a thousand days
choices.why: Right. The backfill becomes a series of `INSERT INTO` statements of a hundred days each.

prompt: Match each part of the setup to what it decides.
hint: Two of them are about files, two about money.

pairs.right: How much of each file a question reads
How many files a question opens
The least a small query is billed
The most one query may read before it is cancelled

right_distractors: How long answers stay in the results prefix

prompt: Put in order what happens between the shop's export and an Athena answer about that day.
hint: Athena reads what the catalog names.
items: The day's CSV lands in the raw bucket
A job writes the day as Parquet under `dt=` in the curated bucket
The partition is added to the catalog
A query filtered on that `dt` reads the day's column blocks

prompt: A dashboard runs `SELECT neighbourhood, count(*) FROM orders_csv WHERE dt BETWEEN '2026-10-01' AND '2026-10-07' GROUP BY neighbourhood` every hour. Which one change cuts what it reads the most?
hint: It already reads only seven days.

choices.text: Point it at the Parquet table `orders` instead
choices.why: Right. The days are already pruned; the format then reads one column of seven instead of whole lines.

choices.text: Run it in a workgroup with a 10 MB cutoff
choices.why: A cutoff cancels a query; it does not make the same question read less.

choices.text: Run `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` before each refresh
choices.why: That registers partitions; the seven days it reads stay the same.

choices.text: Drop the `WHERE` and filter the days in the dashboard
choices.why: Without the filter it would read all 31 days of CSV, four times more.

prompt: A query reads 25,165,825 bytes. Counting a megabyte as 1,048,576 bytes, how many megabytes does Athena bill for it?
hint: Divide, then apply the two rules.
